source.title: How Many Features Can a Language Model Store Under the Linear Representation Hypothesis?
source.authors: Nikhil Garg; Jon M. Kleinberg; Kenny Peng

record.tranche_reason: The paper develops theoretical bounds for abstract linear feature representation and accessibility, but does not test the empirical neuron-pole claims or any listed version.
record.gate_note: The results are mathematical bounds for an abstract linear representation framework, not empirical measurements of neurons in language models. The paper also cites prior empirical work, but those cited results are not this study's results.
record.test_reason: A purely theoretical paper proving bounds on how many sparse features d neurons can linearly store and decode. It audits no real model neurons, measures no shares of interpretable neurons, and does not engage the essay's claims. Its point that superposition is mathematically possible bears only loosely on V3's 'not superposition' framing and tests no version.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors also say the upper bound gives theoretical evidence for the superposition hypothesis. They add that adding a bias and a monotone activation does not increase capacity asymptotically (Theorem 12 and Corollary 13).
record.recipe_differences: The original sources concern empirical neuron interpretability audits; this paper uses mathematical analysis of abstract linear embeddings and sparse feature vectors.

fits_no_version.finding: Under linear representation plus linear decoding, k-sparse features need d between Ω((k²/log k) log(m/k)) and O(k² log m) dimensions. Linear decoding is thus a stronger requirement than nonlinear compressed sensing, which needs O(k log(m/k)), yet exponentially many features in d remain storable.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Under the linear representation hypothesis, a layer of d neurons can store and linearly decode exponentially many sparse features, with a near-quadratic dependence on sparsity k.

record.problems: The evidence is theoretical and depends on the paper's abstract assumptions about linear representation, sparse feature vectors, and linear recovery; it does not empirically validate these assumptions in language models. The supplied rendering of Theorem 3's restriction on ϵ is ambiguous.
record.rows_left_out: No other results were left out. The paper's geometry propositions and binary-classification extension are theoretical results about the same abstract framework, but they do not measure the objects named in any claim version.

untested.parts: All of it: no Qwen3-32B neuron-pole audit or shares.
All of it: no audits of other models or at other scales.
All of it: no InceptionV1 neurons examined. Superposition is shown possible in theory, not shown to occur in real neurons.
All of it: no comparison of architectures, regularization or tools.
All of it: no attribution graphs.
All of it: no neuron explanations tested.
All of it: no automated scoring of explanations.

record.verdict_notes: The record's peer_reviewed field (COLT) is not supported by the text, which shows only an arXiv v1 preprint dated Feb 2026 with no venue. No original source is cited. The geometry propositions (9 and 11) and the binary-classification extension are likewise abstract and bear on no version.

versions.untested_parts: The Qwen3-32B audit, the shares of poles with one or two jobs, and the share not understood.
No audits of other models, dense or mixture-of-experts models, or models up to trillions of parameters; no shares of interpretable neurons are measured.
No InceptionV1 cat-and-car example or test of pose, recursive generalization, or superposition as its explanation.
No comparison of architectures, regularization, tools, or estimates for InceptionV1-sized vision models.
No attribution graphs or test of whether model neurons explain behavior without replacement models or reconstruction error.
No explanations tested on activating examples or measurements of whether they predict where neurons fire.
No automated scoring of neuron explanations on new text.

rows.subject: linear representation framework (A, B ∈ R^{d×m})
rows.operation_detail: Theorem 2 gives an upper bound on embedding dimension sufficient for linear recovery of sparse feature vectors.
rows.measure: sufficient embedding dimension d for linear recovery
rows.note: A theoretical bound for an abstract framework; it does not report an observed capacity in a language model or the share of neurons with interpretable jobs.
rows.check: Link is correct. This is a proven bound for an abstract construction, not a measurement of any model's neurons.
